chapters.name: Chapter 1: What to sell and where

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing what to sell
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick one product or service that fits your skills and audience.
This lesson builds toward: Given what your audience asks you about, you will choose one physical, service or digital product to sell first, with the time and money it needs written down.
Athletes usually sell one of three things. Physical products: T-shirts, hats, stickers or posters with your own design or logo. Services: private lessons, small-group training, camps and clinics. Digital products: training plans, video courses or workout guides.
Start with one thing your audience already asks you about. If parents keep asking about lessons, sell lessons. If fans comment on your logo, try merch.
Think about time and risk. Services pay for your time but need your schedule. Merch needs money up front unless you use print-on-demand. Digital products take time to make but can sell many times.
Step by step:
- List what your audience asks you about.
- Sort ideas into physical, service or digital.
- Note the time and money each needs.
- Pick one to start.
Words to know:
- E-commerce: buying and selling online.
- Print-on-demand: a service that prints and ships an item only after someone orders it.
- Digital product: something sold as a file or online access, like a training plan.
Try it now: List three things people have asked you about. Ask an AI assistant to list pros and cons of selling each, then pick one.
You can now choose one product or service that fits your skills and audience.

check.q: Which of these is a physical product?
options: A T-shirt with your own design
check.why: Physical products include T-shirts, hats, stickers and posters.

check.q: Parents keep asking you about lessons for their kids. What do you try first?
check.why: Start with something your audience already asks about.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Comparing store platforms
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare two platforms and pick one using their current fees and features.
This lesson builds toward: Using two platforms' official pricing pages, you will compare their monthly, per-sale and payment fees and choose one, with the real current fees written down and age rules checked.
You do not need to build a store from scratch. Store builders like Shopify, Square Online and Wix let you list products and take payments. Print-on-demand services such as Printful or Printify connect to stores and handle printing and shipping. For lessons and camps, booking and sign-up tools or a simple payment link can be enough.
Every platform charges in some way: monthly plans, a percentage of each sale, payment processing fees, or all three. These change often, so read each platform's current pricing page and write the real numbers down.
If you are under 18, many platforms and payment services require an adult to own or co-own the account. Involve a parent or guardian.
Step by step:
- Pick two platforms that fit your offer.
- Open each one's official pricing page.
- Write the monthly cost, per-sale fee and payment fee.
- Check age rules.
- Pick the one with the lowest total cost for your expected sales.
Words to know:
- Platform: an online service you use to run your store.
- Processing fee: what a payment service charges to take a card payment.
Try it now: Pick two platforms. From their official pricing pages, write each one's monthly cost and fees in a small table, and pick the cheaper total for 20 sales a month.
You can now compare store platforms by their real, current fees and pick one.

check.q: What do Printful and Printify do?
options: Handle printing and shipping for orders
check.why: Print-on-demand services connect to stores and handle printing and shipping.

check.q: A friend says a platform costs nothing. What do you do?
options: Ask an AI for the price
Read the platform's current pricing page and write down the fees
check.why: Every platform charges in some way, and fees change, so read the current pricing page.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Rules first: NIL, logos and trademarks
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check the rules that apply before selling anything with your name or a logo.
This lesson builds toward: Before selling anything with your name or a logo, you will check the NIL, logo, trademark and tax rules that apply to you, with no school, team or league logo used without written permission, a USPTO search done and the person you checked with named.
Selling things with your own name, image or likeness can count as NIL activity. College athletes may need to report it; NCAA rules say NIL pay must be for a real business purpose and not tied to performance. High school rules vary by state. Ask your compliance office or state athletic association first.
Do not use your school's or team's logo, name, mascot or colors in a way that looks official unless you have written permission. Schools and leagues usually own and protect these. Pro league logos and other brands' logos are also off-limits.
Make your own logo, and search the USPTO trademark records before choosing a brand name to avoid copying someone else's. Selling income is generally taxable; the IRS says you must file if net self-employment earnings are $400 or more, so keep records and talk with a tax professional.
Step by step:
- Ask your compliance office or state association about NIL rules for selling.
- Do not use school, team or league logos without written permission.
- Create your own logo.
- Search USPTO trademark records for your brand name.
- Set up a simple record of sales and costs.
Words to know:
- Trademark: a name, logo or slogan that identifies a business and is protected by law.
- Licensing: official permission to use someone else's logo or name, often for a fee.
Official sources:
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
- USPTO: Trademark basics
- IRS: Self-Employed Individuals Tax Center
Try it now: Write a rules checklist for your product: NIL (who you asked), logos (whose, and permission), trademark search (done or not), and records (where you will keep them).
You can now check NIL, logo, trademark and tax basics before selling.

check.q: Who usually owns a school's logo, mascot and name?
check.why: Schools and leagues usually own and protect these.

check.q: You picked a brand name for your merch. What do you do before printing?
options: Search USPTO trademark records for the name
check.why: Searching USPTO records helps you avoid copying someone else's trademark.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Building and launching your offer

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a product page with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear, honest product page with AI help.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI draft, you will write an honest product page that answers what, who, what you get, price, when and how, under 200 words, with every detail true, real photos you own and clear refund rules.
A product page answers buyers' questions: What is it? Who is it for? What do I get? How much, when and how? For a camp: dates, ages, location, what kids learn, safety, what to bring, and the refund policy.
Ask an AI assistant: "Write a product page for a 1-hour private shooting lesson for players aged 10-16. Include what they'll learn, what to bring, location type, price placeholder, and a short refund policy. Friendly, clear, under 200 words." Then edit every detail to be true.
Use real photos you own. Do not promise results like "guaranteed starter" or make health claims. Clear refund and cancellation rules prevent arguments later.
Step by step:
- List what buyers need to know.
- Ask AI for a page draft under 200 words.
- Check every detail and fix anything untrue.
- Add real photos you own.
- Add clear refund and cancellation rules.
Words to know:
- Product page: the page that describes what you sell and lets people buy it.
- Refund policy: your rules for giving money back.
Try it now: Use AI to draft your product page, then edit it so every detail is true and add a refund policy.
You can now write a clear, honest product page with AI help.

check.q: Which detail belongs on a camp product page?
check.why: Buyers need dates, ages, location, what kids learn, what to bring and refunds.

check.q: AI's draft says your lessons "guarantee a scholarship". What do you do?
options: Remove it; do not promise results
check.why: Do not promise results or make claims you cannot keep.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Pricing from real costs
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a price that covers your costs and leaves a profit.
This lesson builds toward: Given every cost of one sale, you will calculate a price that covers your costs and leaves a profit, with the math checked in a spreadsheet and with a calculator.
Price starts with cost. For merch: the item cost, printing, shipping, platform fees and payment fees. For lessons: facility rental, equipment, travel, your time and fees.
Add up the cost of one sale, then look at what similar products or lessons cost in your area. Choose a price above your cost that your audience can pay. The difference is your profit, before taxes.
Use a spreadsheet: columns for each cost, a total, your price and profit. An AI assistant can set up the formulas, but check the math with a calculator.
Step by step:
- List every cost for one sale.
- Add them up.
- Check what similar offers cost nearby.
- Set a price above cost that fits your audience.
- Check the math in a spreadsheet.
Words to know:
- Cost: the money you spend to make or deliver one sale.
- Profit: price minus all costs, before taxes.
Try it now: Build a pricing sheet for one sale of your product. Ask AI to write the total and profit formulas, then check them with a calculator.
You can now set a price from real costs and know your profit per sale.

check.q: Which is a cost for a private lesson?
check.why: Lesson costs include facility, equipment, travel, your time and fees.

check.q: Your shirt costs 14 to make, ship and sell. Similar shirts nearby sell for 12 to 25. What price makes sense?
options: A price above 14 that your audience can pay, such as 20
check.why: Price above your total cost so there is a profit, within what your audience can pay.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Launching and keeping customers happy
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a small launch and a simple customer service routine.
This lesson builds toward: When your offer is ready, you will plan a soft launch and a customer service routine, with problems fixed before the big announcement and messages answered within a day.
Start small: a soft launch to family, teammates' families and close followers. Fix problems before a big announcement. Then announce with a post, a short video and a link in your bio.
If you post about your own products, that's your business, but if a brand or another person gives you anything to promote them, disclose it clearly. College athletes: report deals on time if required.
Customer service builds repeat buyers: answer messages within a day, ship or confirm bookings on time, follow your refund policy, and say thank you. Ask AI to draft polite reply templates for common questions.
Step by step:
- Soft launch to a small group.
- Fix any problems.
- Announce with a post, a video and a bio link.
- Reply to messages within a day.
- Use AI to draft reply templates.
Words to know:
- Soft launch: a small, quiet first release to catch problems.
- Customer service: how you help buyers before and after they pay.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page launch plan: offer and audience, platform and current fees, AI-drafted product page, price from real costs, and rules checklist with who you checked with.
You can now launch a small online offer and give good customer service.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Offer and audience The product or its audience is unclear. One product or service, who it is for, and the time and money it needs. Shows evidence the audience asked for it, such as comments or parent requests. Platform and fees No fees listed, or fees guessed rather than taken from the pricing page. The chosen platform with its current monthly, per-sale and payment fees from its pricing page, and age rules checked. Compares two platforms and shows the total cost at the expected number of sales. Product page Missing key details, untrue claims, or no refund rules. Under 200 words, answers what, who, what you get, price, when and how, with real photos and clear refund rules. Includes safety details for youth offers and answers to common questions. Price from costs Price is below cost or costs are missing. Every cost of one sale listed, totaled and priced above cost, with the math checked. Shows profit per sale and how many sales cover any upfront costs. Rules checklist NIL, logo, trademark or tax items missing, or no one named. NIL, school logos, trademarks and taxes each checked, with who the athlete checked with. Includes written logo permission or a USPTO search result, and a sales and cost record set up. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Who is a soft launch for?
options: Family, teammates' families and close followers
check.why: Start small and fix problems before the big announcement.

check.q: A customer asks for a refund that fits your refund policy. What do you do?
options: Follow your policy, refund politely and say thank you
check.why: Following your refund policy and replying politely builds repeat buyers.
